brief: A utensil holder with two bins that is waterproof and dishwasher safe.

requirements.evidence: Two 2-storey cells (fused:0,0,0 and fused:1,0,0) with deep bins for standing utensils, end caps on every open face and a joint bolt between the cells. The configurator refused the fork and spoon props, which only lie flat, so the use isn't shown with props.

The configurator checks fit only, not watertightness, which depends on material and printing. The bins I chose have drain holes, which let rinse water out. That helps with drying but means the bins don't hold water.
Whether the parts survive heat and detergent depends on the material the user chooses. The configurator doesn't check this.

finish.summary: I built a two-bin utensil holder: two 2-storey hex cells side by side, each holding a 2-storey drained bin (hex-bin-full-drain-x2, about 160 mm deep). Every open face has an end cap and the joint between the cells is bolted. The configurator's checks pass, with meshes clear. The build has 19 parts and an estimated 1,987 g of filament. I couldn't add utensil props to show its use: the fork and spoon props only lie flat, and the configurator refused to place either one in the bins. I can't claim it is waterproof or dishwasher safe. Those depend on the print material and process, and the configurator doesn't check either.

lines.label: Bin, full depth, drained, 2 stories deep
Edge cap · male, two stories tall
M6 x 25 socket head screw, ISO 4762

notes: Tighten every M6 to 2 N.m: HAND TOOLS ONLY, never a cordless driver. These bolts clamp printed PETG, not metal: at the bolt's own 10.4 N.m rating the head crushes the plastic under it and the joint fails silently, looking tight while holding nothing. Snug, then a nudge. Re-check the bolts after the first few weeks: PETG relaxes under load and the clamp will have eased.
